newsitem.title: UK: Focus set on Matthew Clark trading outlook.
newsitem.headline: Focus set on Matthew Clark trading outlook.

text.p: Full-year results from British cider maker Matthew Clark, whose dramatic share price collapse last September stunned investors, will be closely watched on Wednesday for its current trading update, said analysts.
"It's almost irrelevant what the numbers are as we all know it has been a terrible year for the company," said Eddy Hargreaves an analyst at UBS.
"The real issue will be what current trading is like and how the relaunch of their brands is going," he added.
The company's shares plunged 60 percent from 673 pence after a profits warning in September, stripping more than 290 million stg off its market value.
"Confidence in the management has been shot to pieces in the last year, so any indication that stability is returning to the cider market will be greeted favourably," said Hargreaves.
On Friday the shares were steady around the 238 pence level, compared with a high of 340 pence for the year.
Matthew Clark was forced to put together a recovery plan in January aimed at tackling the phenomenal rise in popularity of so-called alcopops and a severe, industry-wide price war.
It unveiled plans to spend more on advertising, in an effort to rebuild its cider brands, bring back 18- to 24-year old drinkers and strengthen its management team.
"We are now looking to see a greater level of commitment towards their advertising and positioning of their brands," said Nick Williamson, an analyst at Credit Lyonnais Laing.

At the time, the group estimated it would lose 22 million stg over the year from a combination of lower sales and tougher competition over pricing and supply contracts to national and regional brewers.
Sales of its "Diamond White" and "K" crashed some 30 percent due to the emergence of alcopops, costing the group 11 million stg in annual profits.

Analysts expect pre-tax profits for the year to end April 1997 to range from 39-41 million stg, and at the half-year stage the company forecast it would maintain its dividend, making a total 24 pence for the year.
On July 16, Clark's larger rival H.P. Bulmer Holdings reported a 9.2 percent increase in profits before tax and exceptional items to 30.1 million stg in the year ending April 25, 1997.

It also said cider consumption in Britain, at 5.1 million hectolitres, declined by 2.7 percent, but in the six months to June 1997 its sales increased by eight percent, giving it confidence in the underlying strength of the market.

Matthew Clark generates only 45 percent of its profits from cider, with the rest coming from its wholesale business and branded drinks like Strathmore water, as well as the distribution of Miller Genuine Draft beer.
